section.title: To You I Lift Up My Soul
section.sectionRationale: An acrostic psalm of David, its lines following the order of the Hebrew alphabet as a sign of completeness and careful devotion. It moves between plea and confidence: David lifts his soul to the LORD, confesses the sins of his youth, and asks to be taught God's ways, grounding every request in God's covenant loving devotion and His goodness to sinners who fear Him.
section.thesis: David lifts up his soul in trust to the LORD, asking not for an easy path but for instruction in God's ways, pardon for his sin, and deliverance from his enemies, all resting on the changeless loving devotion of a God who guides sinners and confides in those who fear Him.
section.frameNote: Four movements: trust and a plea for guidance despite shame, enemies, and sin (1-7); the LORD's goodness in guiding sinners and the humble (8-11); covenant intimacy with those who fear Him (12-14); and a renewed plea for deliverance, closing with prayer for the whole nation (15-22).

units.label: To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul
units.note: trust and a plea for guidance despite shame, enemies, and sin

verses.text: To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul;
in You, my God, I trust. Do not let me be put to shame; do not let my enemies exult over me.
Surely none who wait for You will be put to shame; but those who are faithless without cause will be disgraced.
Show me Your {{derek|ways}}, O LORD; teach me Your paths.

Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; 
all day long I wait for You.
Remember, O LORD, Your compassion and {{chesed|loving devotion}}, for they are from age to age.
Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my rebellious acts; remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD.

units.label: Good and upright is the LORD
units.note: guidance for sinners and the humble

verses.text: Good and upright is the LORD; therefore He shows sinners the way.
He guides the humble in what is right and teaches them His way.
All the LORD's ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.
For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity, for it is great.

units.label: The LORD confides in those who fear Him

verses.text: Who is the man who fears the LORD? He will instruct him in the path chosen for him.
His soul will dwell in prosperity, and his descendants will inherit the land.
The LORD confides in those who fear Him, and reveals His {{berit|covenant}} to them.

units.label: Redeem Israel, O God
units.note: a renewed plea, widened to the whole nation

verses.text: My eyes are always on the LORD, for He will free my feet from the mesh.
Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted.
The troubles of my heart increase; free me from my distress.
Consider my affliction and trouble, and take away all my sins.
Consider my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with vicious hatred.

Guard my soul and deliver me; let me not be put to shame, 
for I take refuge in You.
May integrity and uprightness preserve me, because I wait for You.
Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.

derek.gloss: Way, road, path, often used of a manner of life or of God's own dealings and instruction. David's plea to be shown God's ways is a plea for moral and relational conformity to God, not merely information, fulfilled in Jesus, who calls Himself the way, John 14:6.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion. David appeals to this quality of God, unchanging from age to age, as the ground for both forgiveness of his youthful sin and confidence that God's ways are trustworthy.

berit.gloss: Covenant, a binding relational commitment. The LORD reveals this covenant to those who fear Him, an intimacy of friendship fulfilled and deepened in the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood, Luke 22:20, Hebrews 8:10.

basic.context: This acrostic psalm follows the Hebrew alphabet line by line, a mark of careful, complete devotion rather than a hurried cry. David lifts his soul to the LORD, asking to be shown God's ways and taught His paths, confessing both present shame and the sins of his youth, and grounding every plea in God's changeless compassion and loving devotion. The psalm widens at its end from David's own trouble to a prayer for the redemption of the whole nation, Israel.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm should be read as a model prayer of humble dependence: guidance from God is not a reward for the sinless but a gift to sinners who fear Him, are humble, and keep covenant with Him. Its acrostic form signals that David means to bring his whole self, from alef to tav, before the LORD.
basic.originalLanguages: David asks to be shown God's derek, ways, and pleads on the basis of God's chesed, His steadfast covenant loving devotion, appealing to it both for pardon of his sins and for confidence in future guidance. The LORD's berit, covenant, is revealed as an intimate friendship to those who fear Him, not a mere legal arrangement.
basic.typology: David's plea to be taught God's ways anticipates Jesus, who does not merely point to the way but declares Himself to be the way, the truth, and the life, John 14:6. The covenant intimacy promised to those who fear the LORD, verse 14, is deepened and secured forever in the new covenant Christ establishes in His blood.
basic.christ: Jesus is the fulfillment of every plea in this psalm. He is the way David longed to be shown, John 14:6, the perfectly humble and upright one who was Himself taught by the Father and always did what pleased Him, John 8:29. He bears the guilt of iniquity great enough to require forgiveness, not His own but ours, and He seals a new and better covenant, revealed not only to the few who feared the LORD under David, but to all who trust in Him, Hebrews 8:10-12.
basic.god: God is shown as approachable to sinners, not despite His goodness but because of it: 'Good and upright is the LORD, therefore He shows sinners the way,' verse 8. His guidance is relational, not mechanical, offered to the humble and those who fear Him, and grounded in covenant loving devotion that reaches back to David's youth and forward to Israel's future redemption.
basic.crossReferences: John 14:6 shows Jesus as the way David sought to be shown. Hebrews 8:10-12 describes the new covenant in which God's ways are written on hearts and sins are remembered no more, the ultimate answer to David's plea in verse 7. Titus 2:11-12 shows God's grace itself teaching believers to live uprightly.
basic.oneStory: David's lifelong plea to be shown God's ways, forgiven his sin, and kept safe by covenant loving devotion finds its answer in Jesus Christ, who is Himself the way, who bears away the guilt too great to forgive on our own, and who seals forever the covenant intimacy David could only long for from a distance.

context.literary:
The acrostic is the psalm's architecture, and it is not perfect. Verse 1 begins with the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet and verse 21 with the last, but the sequence bends in a few places, and the final verse, verse 22, begins with the letter peh, which has already been used, so that it sits outside the alphabet altogether. Psalm 34 ends in the same way, with a closing verse that begins with peh and speaks of redeeming, Psalm 34:22. Scholars also note other small irregularities in the sequence. The bends are worth taking seriously, because they keep the form from being a mere exercise. Whoever wrote the psalm was praying, and let the alphabet give way when the prayer needed it. The last verse, the plea to redeem Israel, is an addition to the alphabet's completeness that lifts the whole prayer beyond one man's need.

An acrostic cannot easily develop a single argument, and the psalm does not march in a straight line. It circles. Three themes recur in different clothes: guidance, forgiveness and rescue from enemies. Verses 4 and 5 ask for guidance, and verses 8 to 10 and 12 to 14 return to it as teaching about God. Verses 6 and 7 ask for pardon, and verse 11 and verse 18 come back to it. Enemies appear in verses 2, 19 and 20. The psalm reads as a prayer that keeps returning to its deepest needs, in the manner of a person who cannot stop praying about what weighs on him.

Within the circling there is a centre. The middle of the psalm, verses 8 to 14, is in the third person and speaks about the LORD, while the parts around it speak to Him, with the plea of verse 11 set in the middle. The prayer is framed by the theology it rests on, and the theology comes at the point where the prayer has become most anxious, with the sins of youth in verse 7 and the great iniquity of verse 11. The psalm reasons its way to confidence by telling itself who God is.

Some words hold the frame together. The verb 'wait' appears in verses 3, 5 and 21, in the Hebrew qavah, and the verb 'remember' is used three times in verses 6 and 7, twice in a plea and once in a refusal. The word 'shame' opens the psalm in verses 2 and 3 and returns in verse 20. The prayer begins with a soul lifted in verse 1 and ends with a nation in need of redeeming in verse 22, moving outward from the individual to the whole people.
context.historical:
The heading gives the psalm to David, and the tradition is credible: the enemies, the loneliness and the sins of youth suit a man whose life ran from shepherd boy to hunted fugitive to king. The psalm does not tell us which crisis it comes from, and its language has none of the marks of a single event. What it does show is that Israel's kings and ordinary worshippers prayed in the same words, since verse 22 turns from the singer's private trouble to 'Israel.'

The acrostic was a favourite form of Israel's teachers and singers. It stands behind Psalms 9 and 10, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119 and 145, and Proverbs 31:10 to 31, and the four laments of Lamentations 1 to 4. Such a form helped memory, and it suggested that the subject had been treated from beginning to end. A worshipper who learned Psalm 25 by heart had, at the same time, learned the alphabet of prayer.

The psalm's central verses draw on the covenant God had shown Moses at Sinai. When the LORD passed before Moses He proclaimed Himself 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,' 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin,' Exodus 34:6 to 7. The vocabulary of Psalm 25 is the same: compassion in verse 6, loving devotion and faithfulness in verse 10, iniquity in verses 11 and 18, and forgiveness. The singer has taken the name God gave at Sinai and made it into a prayer. The phrase 'for the sake of Your name' in verse 11 fits this, since the name Moses heard was a name of mercy.

The promise of verse 13, that the man who fears the LORD will see his descendants 'inherit the land,' is the covenant blessing of Israel's land tenure. To the first hearers the land was not an abstract hope. It was fields and homes under threat from enemies, and to say that the family of the God-fearing would inherit it was to say that the covenant would hold. The theme returns in Psalm 37:11, where the meek inherit the land.

The 'sins of my youth' is a phrase that suggests that Israel understood sin as something that could go back a long way and still be forgiven. It fits a king who knew his own failure and needed a God who does not keep accounts. The verb in the prayer, 'remember not,' asks God to leave a past in the past, which Israel took to be possible because of the character of God revealed at Sinai.
context.canonical:
Psalm 25 has two neighbours whose company shapes the reading. Psalm 24 ends with the King of Glory entering the gates, and its fourth verse speaks of the man who 'does not lift up his soul to an idol.' Psalm 25 begins, 'To You, O LORD, I lift up my soul.' The same Hebrew verb and the same noun are used in both, and it is hard to think the placing accidental. Psalm 24 asks who may ascend; Psalm 25 shows a person doing what the answer asked, lifting his soul to the LORD alone. Psalm 26, on the other side, will speak of walking in integrity, and the phrase 'integrity and uprightness' of Psalm 25:21 hints at it. Psalms 22 to 25 also speak of a solitary sufferer: the 'only one' of Psalm 22:20 and the 'lonely' one of Psalm 25:16 use the same Hebrew root.

The psalm draws on Israel's wisdom as much as its worship. Its promise of teaching to the humble and its blessing on those who fear the LORD are the language of Proverbs. 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom,' Proverbs 9:10, and Proverbs 3:32 says that God 'is a friend to the upright,' which comes close to the LORD confiding in those who fear Him in verse 14. Psalm 86:11, 'Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth,' repeats verse 5, and Psalm 143:8 to 10 gives a like prayer, with a further request for the good Spirit to lead.

The psalm's treatment of sin looks forward to the prophets. It asks God not to remember the sins of youth, and Jeremiah promises the new covenant with the words, 'I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more,' Jeremiah 31:34. The petition of Psalm 25 becomes a promise in Jeremiah, and Hebrews 8:12 and 10:17 quote that promise as fulfilled in Christ. The friendship of verse 14 also resonates with the promise that 'they will all know Me,' Jeremiah 31:34. The last verse looks the same way: God 'will redeem Israel from all iniquity,' Psalm 130:8, and Titus 2:14 says that Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.'

The Sermon on the Mount takes up the psalm's inheritance. 'The meek will inherit the land,' Psalm 37:11, is quoted by Jesus as 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, and the humble of Psalm 25:9 stand in the same line. The New Testament does not cite Psalm 25 by formula, but its themes are carried everywhere: the way, the teaching, the friendship of God, the pardon and the redemption.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted Israel to see that guidance and forgiveness cannot be separated. Verses 4 and 5 ask for a path, and verses 6 and 7 ask for pardon, in the same breath. He does not wait to be clean before asking to be taught, and he does not ask to be taught while quietly holding on to his record. A person who wants to walk in God's truth begins by asking God not to count the past against him.

He wanted them to see where the grounds of the prayer lie. Three times the psalm gives a reason for God to act, and none of the reasons is the singer. He asks for God's compassion, verse 6, for God's goodness, verse 7, and for God's name, verse 11. The Hebrew of verses 7 and 11 says 'for the sake of' twice, first of God's goodness and then of His name. The psalm teaches Israel to argue from who God is.

He wanted them to hear the surprise in verse 8. God is good and upright, and therefore He 'shows sinners the way.' Many would have expected the opposite conclusion: that a God who is upright would turn from sinners. The verse says that His uprightness is the very reason He teaches them. The author meant this to be a message of hope for those who knew they were not righteous.

He also meant to say something about the shape of the good life. Verses 9 to 14 describe the person God instructs: humble, covenant-keeping, one who fears the LORD. These are dispositions of a whole life, and the reward is not a list of things but a relationship, the friendship of verse 14. The psalm's purpose is that Israel should want that intimacy more than success or security.

Finally, the closing verse lifts the reader's eyes. The individual is not left alone, and in the last line the singer's need becomes the nation's, 'from all its distress.' The author wanted a worshipper who prays this psalm to remember that God's dealings with him are a part of God's dealings with His people.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what David prayed and what he came to be confident of. It does not promise that every humble person will inherit a piece of land or see their descendants prosper. Verse 13 is a covenant blessing given to Israel in the land and is to be read within Israel's history. Later voices in the Psalter face the fact that the humble suffer, and the same book holds Psalm 73 and Psalm 88 beside Psalm 25. The blessing is a promise about God's faithfulness. It cannot be turned into a guarantee that a good life brings security.

The psalm also does not say that guidance comes without cost. The teaching is given to those who wait, and the psalm's language, 'all day long I wait for You,' is a reminder that God's answers are not always quick. The reader who treats verse 4 as a formula for finding God's will in a particular decision is asking more of the text than it says. The psalm describes a way of life that keeps returning to God, and it does not give a technique.

What carries forward is the pattern of prayer. The believer is meant to come with confession, to appeal to God's character and not to personal merit, to expect that God will teach the humble, and to wait. The psalm also gives a pattern for what to say about the past: to name the sins of youth, to ask for their pardon, and to ask that God remember us according to His love. New Testament believers pray this in the light of the promise that God 'will remember their sins no more,' Hebrews 8:12, and in the assurance that 'if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us,' 1 John 1:9.

There is also an instruction in the last verse. The psalm tells the worshipper that his own trouble is not the whole of his prayer, and that Israel, and by extension God's people in every age, needs redeeming as well.

debates.question: Is the guidance David seeks in verses 4 and 5 specific direction in a crisis, or a broader request for a life shaped by God's character?

views.label: Specific direction for a real danger
views.case: The psalm speaks of enemies, of feet caught in a net, of loneliness and distress, verses 2, 15 and 19. These are concrete threats, and a man in them would want to know where to go. On this reading the 'paths' are the practical route out of danger, and the request for teaching is a request for wisdom in an emergency.

views.label: A request for a whole way of life
views.case: The words 'ways,' 'paths' and 'truth' are the vocabulary of Israel's moral teaching, and the psalm's centre in verses 8 to 14 speaks of humility, covenant and the fear of the LORD. On this reading the guidance David wants is a character shaped by God, and the enemies are the setting in which he asks.

views.label: Both, since danger drives him to ask for something larger
views.case: A crisis exposes what a person needs most, and the psalm moves from enemy to sin and to God's character. The prayer for a path begins in danger and turns into a prayer for the kind of person God would lead. The reader is not required to choose.

debates.bearing: On all three readings the prerequisite is the same: the guidance is given to the humble who fear the LORD, and no technique replaces the relationship.

debates.question: What does verse 12 mean by 'the path chosen for him'?

views.label: The path God chooses for him
views.case: The BSB reads that the LORD will instruct the man who fears Him 'in the path chosen for him.' The Hebrew verb for 'choose' can mean that God picks the route, and on this reading the God-fearing man is led down a road that God has selected. It fits the picture of a shepherd-like guide and the psalm's stress on being taught and guided.

views.label: The path he should choose
views.case: The same Hebrew can be read with the man as the one who chooses: God will teach him the way 'that he should choose,' as several translations render it. On this view God instructs, and the person decides. It fits the moral character of the teaching, since the man is to make a real choice for God's ways.

debates.bearing: The two readings are complementary. God teaches the way, and the person who fears Him walks it willingly. The verse gives no reason to think that divine guidance overrides a person's will.

debates.question: How can David pray 'May integrity and uprightness preserve me' in verse 21 after confessing great iniquity?

views.label: His own integrity, a fruit of a life that seeks God
views.case: David has confessed sin, but he also claims to wait on God and to take refuge in Him, verses 20 and 21. On this reading he asks that a life of honest devotion, imperfect but real, may count for him and keep him. The words of Psalm 26:1, 'I have walked with integrity,' show that such claims were made by worshippers.

views.label: God's own qualities, as personified guardians
views.case: Verse 8 has said that the LORD is 'good and upright,' and the words of verse 21 are the same ones. Elsewhere in the Psalter God's loving devotion and faithfulness are sent out to guard a person, Psalm 61:7. On this reading David asks that God's uprightness, which he has already described, watch over him.

views.label: An ideal that he prays to have
views.case: The verb is a wish, 'May.' David is not claiming that he has integrity but asking that integrity and uprightness be what surrounds him. The prayer for a life of honesty fits the psalm's larger request to be taught God's way.

debates.bearing: Each reading keeps David from boasting. On the first, his integrity is offered humbly. On the second and third, the credit goes to God. The New Testament view that God supplies what He requires supports the last two.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says 'I lift up my soul,' using the verb nasa, to lift or carry, with 'soul,' nephesh, as its object. The same verb and noun appear in Psalm 24:4, where the person who may ascend the hill is the one who 'does not lift up his soul to an idol.' They appear again in Psalm 143:8, 'to You I lift up my soul.' The gesture is a directing of the whole self, the life and its desires, toward one object. What David lifts in verse 1 is his whole person, and the same verb returns in verse 18, where he asks God to lift away his sins, so that David lifts his soul to God and asks God to lift his guilt.

In verses 3, 5 and 21 the psalm says 'wait,' from the verb qavah. The word has a picture in it, a cord stretched tight, so that waiting is a matter of tension and hope, not of idleness. In Isaiah 40:31 the same verb appears in the promise that those who wait on the LORD will renew their strength. The BSB footnote at verse 21 offers 'because my hope is in You' as an alternative, which is a reminder that in Hebrew waiting and hoping are one thing.

The verb 'remember,' zakar, is used in verses 6 and 7 three times and in two directions: 'Remember, O LORD, Your compassion,' 'Remember not the sins of my youth,' 'remember me according to Your loving devotion.' To remember in Hebrew is more than to recall. It is to act on what one recalls. David therefore asks God to act on His mercy and not to act on his sin. The word for 'compassion' in verse 6, rachamim, is built on the word for the womb, and it means the tenderness of a parent for a child.

In verses 8 and 12 the LORD 'shows' sinners the way and 'instructs' the man who fears Him. Both words are forms of yarah, the verb that also stands behind torah, the teaching. God's guidance is torah, given by a Teacher and not shouted by a commander. The word for 'guides' in verse 9 is a verb formed from the word for the way, and it means to make someone walk it. The humble, anavim, are those who are bowed low. Numbers 12:3 uses the word of Moses, 'a very humble man,' and Zephaniah 2:3 calls the humble to seek the LORD.

In verse 11 'forgive' is salach, a verb that in the Old Testament is used only of God. No one else forgives in this sense. The reason given, 'for it is great,' means that the iniquity is large, and David does not shrink it. The pardon rests on God's name.

Verse 14 says the LORD 'confides,' from sod, a word for a circle of intimate counsel, the inner group who share a person's plans. Amos 3:7 uses it when it says that God does 'nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets,' and Proverbs 3:32 says that God is 'a friend to the upright.' Genesis 18:17 shows the same thing when the LORD asks, 'Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?' The psalm puts that Abraham-like friendship within reach of those who fear Him.

In verse 15 the 'mesh' is a net, resheth, a hunter's snare. The same picture is in Psalm 9:15. Verse 16 calls David 'lonely,' yachid, 'alone' or 'only,' the root that stands behind the 'precious life,' literally 'only one,' of Psalm 22:20. In verse 17 the verb hirchivu comes from the word for 'wide,' and it sits beside 'troubles,' a word from the root for narrow. The line can be read as saying that the troubles have grown wide, or as a plea to make the straits wide, and translations divide. Psalm 4:1 uses the same verb of a relief already given: 'You have relieved my distress.'

The last verse's 'Redeem,' padah, is the verb for ransoming, used of the firstborn in Exodus 13 and of Israel in Psalm 130:7 to 8, 'He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.'

typology.type: The sins of youth that God is asked not to remember, verses 7 and 18
typology.fulfillment: David prays that God will not remember his sins and that He will lift them away, verse 18. The prophet turns the prayer into a promise: 'I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more,' Jeremiah 31:34. Hebrews quotes that promise twice and says it is met in the sacrifice of Christ, Hebrews 8:12 and 10:17. Paul explains how God can do this and remain just: Christ was presented 'as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood,' Romans 3:25 to 26. The type falls short because David's pardon was a hope, while for the believer it is a settled fact that rests on a finished work, Hebrews 10:14.

typology.type: The sins that God is asked to lift, verse 18
typology.fulfillment: The verb behind 'take away' in verse 18 is the verb 'to lift or carry.' Isaiah uses it of the Servant: 'He bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12. John the Baptist points at Jesus and says, 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' John 1:29, and Peter says that He 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. David lifted his soul and asked God to lift his sin, and Christ lifts it. The type falls short because David could only ask, while Christ carried the weight into death.

typology.type: The LORD who confides in those who fear Him, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: God took Abraham into His counsel, Genesis 18:17, and spoke to Moses 'as a man speaks to his friend,' Exodus 33:11. These were the rare few. Jesus opens that friendship to His disciples: 'I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you,' John 15:15. The covenant intimacy of verse 14 becomes the ordinary condition of the believer through the Spirit, who reveals what God has prepared, 1 Corinthians 2:9 to 10. The type falls short because the friendship of the Old Testament was for prophets and patriarchs, but the friendship of Christ reaches the least in the church.

typology.type: The humble who inherit the land, and Israel redeemed, verses 9, 13 and 22
typology.fulfillment: The humble are guided, and their children inherit the land. Jesus, who is 'gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29, says that 'the meek will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, and the promise widens from Canaan to the whole creation, Revelation 21:7. The plea to redeem Israel from all distress is answered when God 'has visited and redeemed His people,' Luke 1:68, and Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness,' Titus 2:14. The type falls short because the land of the psalm could be lost to exile, and the distress it names was political, while the redemption in Christ reaches the root of sin.

study.christ:
Psalm 25 leads to Christ most clearly in the two verbs that hold its ends together, the lifting of the soul and the lifting of sin. David begins by lifting his soul to the LORD and asks in verse 18 that God lift all his sins. The word he uses is the plain Hebrew word for lifting and carrying. It is the same word Isaiah uses of the Servant who 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, and the Greek of John 1:29 has a matching verb in 'takes away.' The prayer of a sinner who asks God to carry what he cannot carry is answered in the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Peter says that He 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. The psalm expresses a need that only one Person can meet.

The prayer to be pardoned 'for the sake of Your name' has an answer in the cross as well. The question hanging behind verse 11 is how a God who is upright can forgive iniquity that is 'great.' Verse 8 had said that His uprightness is the reason He teaches sinners, and Paul shows the reason in the death of Christ: God presented Him 'as the atoning sacrifice,' 'to demonstrate His righteousness,' 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:25 to 26. God's name, in the sense of His character, is vindicated by the cross, and forgiveness is granted for the sake of His name.

The psalm leads to Christ also through the figure of the humble one who is taught. Jesus says that He does nothing on His own 'but speak exactly what the Father has taught Me,' and that He always does what pleases the Father, John 8:28 to 29. He is 'gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29, the perfect example of the anavim the psalm says God guides. At the same time He is more than an example. He says, 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6, and so the 'ways' and the 'truth' that David asked to be shown are found in a Person and not only in a path.

The promise of verse 14, that the LORD confides in those who fear Him, is carried by Christ to the church. 'I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you,' John 15:15. The intimacy that was rare in the Old Testament is now the portion of the believer. Jeremiah's new covenant, in which 'they will all know Me,' Jeremiah 31:34, is the same thing at a national scale.

The last line leads to Him too. The plea to redeem Israel from all its distress is answered in the One who 'has visited and redeemed His people,' Luke 1:68. On the road to Emmaus the disciples say, 'We were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel,' Luke 24:21, and the risen Lord then opens the Scriptures to them, Luke 24:27.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm is a prayer of David, and its enemies, its loneliness and its sins are his. We should not put every line in Christ's mouth. In particular, the confession of sin in verse 7 and verse 11 cannot be said by the sinless Son, and the New Testament does not ask us to. The psalm leads to Christ as the answer to what it asks, and not as the voice praying every line.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 25 is a teacher. The psalm asks Him to show, to teach and to guide, and it describes Him as one who instructs sinners, guides the humble and instructs the man who fears Him. The Hebrew for 'show' and 'instruct' comes from the root that also gives torah, the teaching. This is a God who does not leave His people to guess. He also teaches those who have no claim on Him, and that is the surprising centre of the psalm: sinners are taught because God is good and upright.

He is good, and His goodness is the reason He teaches sinners, not a weakness in His holiness. Verse 8 joins the two attributes with a 'therefore.' This corrects a picture in which mercy has to be squeezed out of a reluctant judge. In the psalm mercy comes from the same source as righteousness. The theology matters for the worshipper, since it means that the people who come to God with great iniquity are not approaching a God who is embarrassed by them.

He is faithful to His covenant, and the psalm claims that all His paths are loving and faithful to those who keep it, verse 10. His compassion and love are 'from age to age,' verse 6, which means that David's God is the God of the fathers and does not change. The God who was compassionate to Israel in Exodus 34 is compassionate to a single man now.

He is a God who remembers and who does not, according to His will. The psalm asks Him to remember His mercy and to forget the sins of youth. That says something about God's memory: He is not bound by a ledger. He acts on love. The Old Testament teaches elsewhere that God 'has not dealt with us according to our sins,' Psalm 103:10, and 'as far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions,' Psalm 103:12. Psalm 25 asks for that removal.

He is a friend and confider, verse 14, and the friendship carries an ethical expectation: the humble and the God-fearing. God is not manipulated by a person's need, and He is not distant from it. He gives His counsel to those who revere Him. That combination of fear and friendship is the psalm's largest claim about God.

He is a Redeemer, verse 22. The God who is asked to show the way is also asked to redeem, to ransom, and the psalm assumes that He can and will. The plea belongs to a God who has already redeemed Israel from Egypt and is asked to do it again.

He also waits for us to wait. The psalm's 'all day long I wait for You' assumes a God whose timing is His own, and it does not treat delay as a sign of absence. That is a hard part of the doctrine, and the psalm does not explain it. It gives the worshipper a posture: hope, in the sense of a cord held taut.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to begin with the lifting of the soul, to appeal to what God has revealed about Himself, and to ask for the lifting of sin. It also teaches us to pray for the whole people, and to leave the outcome with a God who is good, upright and near.

crossReferences.note: The name God proclaimed to Moses: compassionate, gracious, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. Psalm 25:6 to 11 is built from these words. The singer takes the revelation at Sinai and prays it back, and he asks for pardon on the grounds of God's own self-description.

The man who may ascend the LORD's hill 'does not lift up his soul to an idol.' The same verb and noun appear in Psalm 25:1, 'I lift up my soul.' Psalm 25 reads as a person doing what Psalm 24's answer required, and the placing of the two shows a deliberate link.

A prayer in the same mould: 'Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul,' and a request that God's good Spirit lead on level ground. It repeats the pairing of lifted soul and asked-for teaching, and adds the Spirit as the guide, which the New Testament develops.

'Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth. Give me an undivided heart.' It matches Psalm 25:5 and shows that the request to be taught was a stock prayer of Israel's worship. The added request for an undivided heart states what the teaching aims at.

'The meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity.' It carries the promise of Psalm 25:13 that the descendants of the God-fearing will inherit the land. Jesus quotes the verse in the Beatitudes, Matthew 5:5, and widens its scope.

'Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?' The LORD takes Abraham into His counsel, which is what Psalm 25:14 says He does with those who fear Him. The psalm makes Abraham's privilege the pattern for every God-fearing worshipper.

The new covenant: God's law written on hearts, everyone knowing Him, and iniquity forgiven with sin remembered no more. Psalm 25:7 and 14 ask for these very things, pardon that forgets and a covenant that is known. The prophet turns the psalm's plea into a promise.

The Servant 'bore the sin of many.' The Hebrew verb is the one David uses when he asks God to lift away his sins in Psalm 25:18. It shows how the language of a sinner's prayer is taken up in the prophecy of one who carries sin in the sinner's place.

'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' John the Baptist announces the answer to the request of Psalm 25:18 that God lift all sin. The verb in John's Greek means 'to lift and remove,' and it pairs naturally with the psalm's Hebrew verb.

Jesus says that He calls His disciples friends because He has made known to them everything He learned from the Father. It is the counterpart of the LORD confiding in those who fear Him in Psalm 25:14, and it brings that privilege from a few patriarchs to all believers.

'He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.' Psalm 25 ends by asking God to redeem Israel from all its distress. The two psalms use the same verb for ransoming and both turn from the individual to the nation, and Psalm 130 shows the deeper need, iniquity, that lies under distress.

The first pair 'were not ashamed.' Psalm 25 prays three times not to be put to shame, verses 2, 3 and 20, using the same root. A prayer that begins in shame looks back to the loss of Eden's openness, and the psalm asks God to restore what sin took away.

Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession.' It answers the last verse of Psalm 25, the plea to redeem from all distress, and reaches to the root of sin, the true trouble beneath every other.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 25 is the prayer of someone outside Eden asking for the way back. The Bible's first story ended with the pair ashamed and hiding, and with the way to the tree of life guarded, Genesis 3:24. The Hebrew word for 'way' in that verse is the same word Psalm 25 asks God to show. The prayer 'Do not let me be put to shame' comes from the far side of the loss described in Genesis 3, since the first pair had been 'not ashamed,' Genesis 2:25, and their shame began with the fall. The singer wants two things Genesis 3 took away: an open road and a face that need not hide.

It also looks back to Sinai. The name God gave to Moses is behind verses 6 to 11, and the covenant with its decrees is behind verse 10. The psalm shows what Israel had learned to do with that name: to pray it. It looks back to Abraham as well, since verse 14 is the friendship of Genesis 18, and to the promise of land in verse 13. The psalm is a small chart of the whole Old Testament story compressed into a prayer: creation and loss, covenant and land, sin and pardon.

It sets up what follows by leaving its requests open. David asks that sins be lifted and remembered no more, but the sacrifices of Israel could not do this finally, Hebrews 10:4. He asks that Israel be redeemed from all distress, and Israel's history goes on with exile and return and further distress. The prophets take the requests and turn them into promises: a new covenant in which sin is remembered no more, a Servant who bears the sin of many, a God who will redeem Israel from all iniquity. The psalm is an unfinished prayer waiting to be answered.

The answer arrives in Christ. He is the way, John 14:6, and He is the one who carries sin, John 1:29. He seals the new covenant in His blood, and He calls His people friends. The path that was guarded in Genesis 3 is opened by 'the new and living way' through the curtain of His body, Hebrews 10:19 to 20. His people, taught by the Spirit, walk it, and they are led as David asked, in God's truth.

The new creation completes the prayer. There the humble inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, and the one who overcomes 'will inherit all things,' Revelation 21:7. Shame is gone, since God 'will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth,' Isaiah 25:8. The people who waited 'all day long' see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the Redeemer who was asked to redeem Israel from all its distress has done it. The alphabet is complete, and the last letter belongs to God.

sermon.title: The Goodness of God and the Guidance of Sinners
sermon.why: Piper walks through Psalm 25's situation of fear, loneliness, guilt, and confusion, showing that the prerequisite for divine guidance is not a quest for messages but a quest for holiness, humility, covenant keeping, and faith, exactly the movement of this psalm.

quiz.q: What does David ask God not to remember, and what does he ask Him to remember, in verses 6-7?

options.text: Not to remember the sins of his youth and rebellious acts, but to remember him according to God's loving devotion and goodness.
options.note: David explicitly contrasts these in verse 7, appealing to God's character rather than his own record.

options.text: Not to remember his sins in general, but to remember his prayers.
options.note: Close, since forgetting sin is half the picture, but verse 7 specifically grounds remembrance in God's loving devotion and goodness, not in the merit of David's prayers.

options.text: Not to remember his youth at all, but to remember his old age.
options.note: This misreads 'sins of my youth' as merely a life stage rather than specific transgressions requiring forgiveness.

options.text: Not to remember Israel's history, but to remember David's kingship.
options.note: The psalm's concern here is personal sin and God's character, not national history or David's throne.

quiz.q: According to verses 8-9, whom does the LORD guide and instruct in His way?

options.text: Sinners and the humble.
options.note: Verse 8 says He shows sinners the way, and verse 9 says He guides the humble; sinlessness is never presented as a qualification for guidance.

options.text: Only kings and rulers.
options.note: The text specifies sinners and the humble, not a particular social class or office.

options.text: Those who show at least some humility, even if still sinful.
options.note: Close, since humility is named in verse 9, but this option narrows the scope; the text also explicitly names sinners generally in verse 8, not only the partly humble.

options.text: Israel's priests exclusively.
options.note: The psalm speaks broadly of sinners and the humble, not a priestly office specifically.

quiz.q: What does verse 14 reveal about the LORD's disposition toward those who fear Him?

options.text: He confides in them, an intimate friendship, and reveals His covenant to them.
options.note: This verse pictures a relational closeness, not merely rule-following, between God and those who fear Him.

options.text: He keeps them at a distance until they prove themselves.
options.note: The verse describes confiding intimacy, the opposite of distance.

options.text: He reveals His covenant only to prophets.
options.note: The verse specifies those who fear Him generally, not a prophetic office specifically.

options.text: He tests them without ever drawing near.
options.note: While the fear of the LORD does involve reverence, this option misses the explicit intimacy of 'confides' and 'reveals.'

quiz.q: What is the psalm's final petition in verse 22?

options.text: That God would redeem Israel from all its distress, widening David's personal prayer to the whole covenant community.
options.note: The psalm ends by broadening from David's individual plea to the nation as a whole.

options.text: That God would give David greater wealth.
options.note: The final verse is about national redemption from distress, not personal wealth.

options.text: That God would deliver David personally, without mentioning the nation.
options.note: Close, since personal deliverance runs through the whole psalm, but verse 22 specifically widens the request to all Israel, not David alone.

options.text: That David alone would be spared, apart from the nation.
options.note: The verse explicitly widens the scope to all Israel, the opposite of sparing David apart from the nation.

quiz.q: What does this psalm teach about the relationship between guidance and holiness?

options.text: Guidance is not earned by sinlessness but is given to those who humble themselves, fear the LORD, and keep covenant with Him.
options.note: Verses 8-14 make clear that humility and the fear of the LORD, not a flawless record, are the conditions for God's guidance.

options.text: Guidance is only available to those who have never sinned.
options.note: The psalm explicitly says the LORD shows sinners the way, verse 8.

options.text: Guidance requires strict religious performance rather than a humble, fearing heart.
options.note: Close, since covenant keeping is named in verse 10, but the psalm frames this as sincere fear and humility rather than flawless religious performance.

options.text: Guidance is unrelated to a person's spiritual condition.
options.note: The psalm ties guidance directly to humility and the fear of the LORD, so spiritual condition is central, not irrelevant.

questions: David asks God to remember His loving devotion rather than the sins of his youth. What sins from your own past do you find hardest to believe God has truly forgiven?
Verse 8 says God shows sinners the way because He is good and upright, not despite it. How does this change the way you approach God when you need guidance but feel disqualified by your own failures?

The psalm ties guidance to humility and the fear of the LORD rather than technique or special messages. Where in your life are you seeking a shortcut to guidance instead of the slower path of humility and holiness?

Verse 14 pictures the LORD confiding in those who fear Him, an intimate friendship. How well does your own picture of God match this kind of relational nearness, rather than a distant, transactional one?

The psalm widens from David's personal plea to a prayer for the whole nation's redemption. Who in your circle of family, friends, or community needs you to carry them in prayer the way David carried Israel?

translationNotes.note: Loving devotion renders chesed, God's steadfast covenant love, appealed to here as unchanging from age to age, the ground for both pardon and confidence.
Sins of my youth likely refers to specific earlier failures rather than a general reference to youthfulness, since David asks God to remember him instead 'according to Your loving devotion.'

Confides renders a Hebrew word for intimate counsel or friendship, the same idea used of close, trusted relationships, picturing God's covenant revealed as personal nearness rather than distant information.
